questions.q: What is the total physical-qubit cost for Scenario 1 (50 logical qubits at distance 11, 241 physical qubits per logical qubit)?
questions.explain: 50 x 241 = 12,050, the directly computed total for Scenario 1.

questions.q: What is the total physical-qubit cost for Scenario 2 (20 logical qubits at distance 27, 1,457 physical qubits per logical qubit)?
questions.explain: 20 x 1,457 = 29,140, the directly computed total for Scenario 2.

questions.q: Why does Scenario 2 cost more total physical qubits than Scenario 1, despite needing fewer logical qubits (20 vs 50)?
options: Its much higher code distance (27 vs 11) costs over 6x more physical qubits per logical qubit, which more than offsets having fewer logical qubits to protect
Scenario 2 actually costs less than Scenario 1; the lesson's numbers are reversed
Logical qubit count has no effect on total cost in either scenario
Code distance has no effect on cost; only logical-qubit count matters
questions.explain: 1,457/241 is roughly 6.05x more per-logical-qubit cost at distance 27 versus distance 11, which dominates over the smaller logical-qubit count in Scenario 2.

questions.q: What general lesson does comparing Scenario 1 and Scenario 2 teach about resource estimation?
options: The target logical error rate (which sets required code distance) typically dominates total physical-qubit cost more than raw logical-qubit count does
Logical-qubit count always matters more than code distance in every case
Code distance and logical-qubit count always contribute equally to total cost
Total cost is independent of both code distance and logical-qubit count
questions.explain: The scenarios directly illustrate that a higher required distance (driven by reliability needs) can dominate total cost even when fewer logical qubits are needed.

questions.q: What is the reusable two-step method this lab demonstrates for estimating physical-qubit cost?
options: Look up (or compute via 2d^2-1) the physical-qubit cost per logical qubit at the chosen distance, then multiply by the number of logical qubits needed
Always assume exactly 9 physical qubits per logical qubit regardless of distance
Measure the actual qubits on real hardware and count them directly
Use the Gidney & Ekera figure directly for every algorithm, regardless of its actual structure
questions.explain: Both scenarios in this lab, and the worked example in the prior lesson, follow this same two-step multiplication method using the lesson 24 cost table.
